title: McGuffey's Second Eclectic Reader
sourceTitle: McGuffey's Second Eclectic Reader, Revised Edition
author: William Holmes McGuffey
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg eBook #14668: 'Public domain in the USA.' Revised edition first copyrighted 1879 (Van Antwerp, Bragg & Co.); renewals 1896, 1907, and 1920, all before 1930.
description: The classic Second Reader: 71 short stories, poems, and nature lessons about brave dogs, honest children, bees, owls, and snowstorms. Each day your child practices a few new words, reads the lesson aloud, copies a line, and narrates it back. The full text is free online.
includes: 72 lessons in 9 units: the introduction plus all 71 Second Reader lessons
Link to the free full text for every lesson
Key new words, a copywork line, and a narration activity each day
Script (cursive) lessons and poems marked in the notes

lessons.title: Getting Started: Sounds and Punctuation
steps: Read through the Articulation tables together, saying each sound clearly
Copywork: “Where is John going?”
Find a period, a question mark, and an exclamation mark in the Punctuation page and say what each one tells the reader
questions: What mark goes at the end of a question?
What mark shows strong feeling?
lessons.notes: The book's introductory pages. Use the sound tables for a few minutes of drill before lessons all year.

lessons.title: Lesson I: Evening at Home
steps: New words: newspaper, stockings, branches, events, story
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “The fire burns brightly.”
Narrate: what is each person in the family doing?
questions: What season is it?
What is the mother doing?

lessons.title: Lesson II: Bubbles
steps: New words: beautiful, rainbow, burst, sneeze, colors, soap
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “See how high it floats in the air!”
Blow bubbles and count the colors you see
questions: Where did Willie's bubble land?
How many colors are in a bubble, according to Harry?
answers: On the cat's face, and it made her sneeze
As many as in the rainbow

lessons.title: Lesson III: Willie's Letter
steps: New words: rubber, parlor, street, number, o'clock
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “Now, please don't forget to come.”
Write a short letter of your own to someone in the family
questions: Who is Willie's letter to?
What two things does Willie ask for?
What time will Willie go to bed?
answers: A gun that will shoot and a rubber ball
lessons.notes: Script page: the whole lesson is printed in cursive handwriting (an image in the online text). Read it together, then use a few lines as copywork.

lessons.title: Lesson IV: The Little Star
steps: New words: above, world, diamond, twinkle, blazing, dew
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “Twinkle, twinkle, little star”
Memorize the first verse; look for stars tonight
questions: What does the star look like in the sky?
When does the star show its light?
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson V: Two Dogs
steps: New words: Newfoundland, terrier, noble, shaggy, friskily, cellar
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “Sport is a good watchdog.”
Compare the two dogs: draw a line down a page and list facts about each
questions: What are the two dogs' names?
Why is the terrier called Dodger?
What did Dodger spoil?

lessons.title: Lesson VI: Afraid in the Dark
steps: New words: between, bureau, needle, afraid, shadow
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “The dark is only a big shadow.”
Make hand shadows on a wall with a lamp
questions: What did mamma ask Willie to get?
How did mamma show him what the dark is?
answers: She made a shadow with her hand
lessons.notes: Ends with a short slate exercise.

lessons.title: Lesson VII: Baby Bye
steps: New words: spiders, tickling, crawls, speck, secret, believe
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “Little fly, good day.”
Look closely at a fly or ant (or a picture) and count its legs
questions: How many legs does the fly have?
What does the poem warn the fly about?
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson VIII: Puss and Her Kittens
steps: New words: servant, attic, cellar, anxious, trouble, dozen
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “Be ever ready to help one another.”
Narrate the story in order, using 'first, then, at last'
questions: Where did Puss want her kittens?
Who finally carried the kittens up?

lessons.title: Lesson IX: Kitty and Mousie
steps: New words: mousie, frolic, spied, pearl, teeth, slipped
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “Long time ago.”
Clap along with the repeated line each time it comes
questions: What color was the kitty?
Did the kitty keep the mousie?
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson X: At Work
steps: New words: precious, game, harm, washed, brushed
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “One thing at a time.”
Talk about how your child can finish work before play today
questions: What did the boy do after play?
What was the boy's saying?
answers: Washed up, then helped his mother, read, or wrote on his slate

lessons.title: Lesson XI: What a Bird Taught
steps: New words: topmost, bough, spray, mate, rosy, answer
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “Little bird so gray”
Read the questions, and let your child chirp the bird's answer
questions: What color is the bird?
What was all the bird would say?
lessons.notes: Poem by Alice Cary. Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XII: Susie Sunbeam
steps: New words: brightness, pleasant, ragged, playmates, unkind, gladness
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “Susie was always pleasant in her play.”
Narrate: how did Susie help the poor little girl?
questions: What was Susie's real name?
Why was she called Sunbeam?
What did Susie give the poor girl?
answers: She had a sweet, smiling face and brought brightness
A nice dress and a pair of shoes

lessons.title: Lesson XIII: If I Were a Sunbeam
steps: New words: woodlands, lilies, drooping, hovels, upward, divine
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “I would shine and shine.”
Name one way your child can be a 'sunbeam' to someone today
questions: What would the sunbeam do for the lilies?
answers: Shine on them until each raised its drooping head
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XIV: Henry, the Bootblack
steps: New words: support, dollar, honest, blacking, gentlemen, earned
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “Black your boots, sir, please?”
Narrate: how did Henry earn money to help his family?
questions: How did Henry get his first dollar?
What did he buy with it?
answers: A man gave it to him for finding his lost pocketbook
A box, three brushes, and some blacking

lessons.title: Lesson XV: Don't Wake the Baby
steps: New words: tread, whisper, softly, careful, cheerful
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “We must not talk, but whisper low.”
Read the poem in a whisper, as if a baby were sleeping
questions: Why must the children tread softly?
Who is coming home to tea?
lessons.notes: Script page: the whole lesson is printed in cursive handwriting (an image in the online text). Read it together, then use a few lines as copywork.

lessons.title: Lesson XVI: A Kind Brother
steps: New words: heavy, middle, handle, brother, deceived
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “I will not do what is wrong.”
Try carrying a bag on a broom handle with someone to feel the difference
questions: What did the boys put under the basket's handle?
Where did the older boy slide the basket?
answers: Near his own end, so his side was heavier

lessons.title: Lesson XVII: My Good-for-Nothing
steps: New words: busy, mischief, ringlets, ponder, embrace
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “Good to love you, mamma.”
Ask your child the poem's question: what are you good for?
questions: What answer did the little boy give?
lessons.notes: Poem by Emily Huntington Miller. Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XVIII: The Kingbird
steps: New words: berries, robin, eagle, hawk, foe, active
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “Is not the little fellow a brave bird?”
Look up a picture of a kingbird and compare its size to a robin
questions: How big is the kingbird?
Why is he called the kingbird?
answers: He can drive off all other birds

lessons.title: Lesson XIX: Evening Hymn
steps: New words: nigh, shadows, darkness, angels
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “Now the day is over”
Read or sing it together at bedtime
questions: What will soon be asleep, according to the hymn?
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XX: The Quarrel
steps: New words: quarrel, agree, settle, kernel, equal, divided
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “This is the way in which quarrels are very apt to end.”
Act it out with a real nut
questions: Why did each boy think the nut was his?
Who got the kernel?
answers: John saw it first; James picked it up first

lessons.title: Lesson XXI: The Bee
steps: New words: creatures, drones, workers, queen, hive, cells, wax
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “The cells are not round, but have six sides.”
Draw a honeycomb of six-sided cells
questions: What are the three kinds of bees?
How many sides does each cell have?
lessons.notes: Ends with a slate exercise.

lessons.title: Lesson XXII: The Song of the Bee
steps: New words: blossoms, clover, fragrant, thistle, meadow, treasure
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “Buzz! buzz! buzz!”
Buzz the refrain together each time it comes
questions: What does the bee do on sunny days?
What does the bee do on cloudy days?
lessons.notes: Poem by Marian Douglas. Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIII: The Torn Doll
steps: New words: heedless, careless, effects, annoy, blame, harshly
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “Put your things away when you are through playing.”
Tidy one shelf or toy box together
questions: Who tore Mary's doll?
Why shouldn't Mary blame the dog?
answers: She left the doll where he could get it

lessons.title: Lesson XXIV: Sheep-Shearing
steps: New words: thoroughly, shearer, dyed, spun, woven, wool
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “It is then dyed, spun, and woven into cloth.”
Look at a wool sweater or yarn and trace its steps back to the sheep
questions: In what month are sheep sheared?
What is done to the wool after it is cut?
answers: It is dyed, spun, and woven into cloth

lessons.title: Lesson XXV: The Clouds
steps: New words: wander, bearers, sultry, grain, rays
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “We are bearers of the rain.”
Go outside and describe today's clouds
questions: What do the clouds carry?
How do clouds help on hot summer days?
answers: They guard us from the sun's rays
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVI: Patty and the Squirrel
steps: New words: forest, squirrel, tame, hollow, snug, shoulder
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “She made them her friends.”
Narrate: how did Patty tame the squirrels?
questions: How did Patty make the squirrels her friends?
Where do squirrels live in winter?
answers: She was quiet and gentle and left crumbs for them
In a hollow in an old tree

lessons.title: Lesson XXVII: The Sparrow
steps: New words: sparrow, frightened, shocking, robbing, ripest, breakfast
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “Come to see me every day.”
Put out crumbs for the birds
questions: What does Thomas say the sparrow steals?
What does the child give the sparrow?
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVIII: Sam and Harry
steps: New words: afternoon, carriage, hedge, truly, supper
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “Which of the boys do you think was truly kind?”
Answer the question at the end of the lesson and tell why
questions: Why didn't Sam give the blind man money?
What did Harry do with the cents?
Who found the money for the blind man?
answers: He had spent it all on his book

lessons.title: Lesson XXIX: The Little Rill
steps: New words: rill, village, rippling, fringe, brink, course
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “Run, run, thou tiny rill.”
Explain 'rill' (a tiny stream); find one on a walk or a map
questions: What does the rill turn?
Who will join the rill's song?
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XXX: The Boat Upset
steps: New words: hastened, possible, balance, boatman, danger, several
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “Sit still, children.”
Talk about safety rules for boats and water
questions: Why did Edgar fall into the water?
Who saved everyone?
answers: He lost his balance trying to get Thomas's stick

lessons.title: Lesson XXXI: Mary's Letter
steps: New words: rowing, drowned, tripped, cousin
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “A man in another boat picked us up.”
Compare the letter with Lesson XXX: what is the same story?
questions: Who is Mary writing to?
What happened to the boat?
answers: It upset, and they were all in the water
lessons.notes: Script page: the whole lesson is printed in cursive handwriting (an image in the online text). Read it together, then use a few lines as copywork. It retells the story of Lesson XXX.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXII: The Tiger
steps: New words: giant, stripes, prey, whiskers, tigress, collar
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “The tiger is a giant cat.”
Find a cat's whiskers (or a picture) and talk about what they are for
questions: What do a tiger's whiskers help it know?
Who took the tiger kitten from the tent?
answers: When something is in its way

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIII: The Fireside
steps: New words: fireside, sewing, knitting, crackle, usual, instructive
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “We feel happy because we have been busy.”
Do a small useful task together and talk about how it feels
questions: What were the girls doing by the fire?
Why did they feel happier tonight?
answers: They had been doing something useful

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIV: Birdie's Morning Song
steps: New words: dewdrops, laziest, slumber, patience, instead
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “Wake up, little darling, wake up!”
Say the refrain together each time it comes
questions: What finally wakes the child?
lessons.notes: Poem by George Cooper. Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXV: Willie and Bounce
steps: New words: strolled, ripples, circle, floating, however
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “Two fast friends were Willie Brown and his little dog Bounce.”
Predict: how will Bounce 'tell' Willie's father?
questions: Where did Willie go with Bounce?
Why did Willie fall in?
answers: The log he stood on turned
lessons.notes: Part one of a two-part story.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVI: Willie and Bounce (Concluded)
steps: New words: yelp, distress, scratched, barking, clothes
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “Bounce started for the river.”
Narrate the whole two-part story
questions: Where did Bounce run for help?
Who saved Willie?

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVII: The Kitchen Clock
steps: New words: talkative, patient, truthful, obliging, improve
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “Life is short, improve it well.”
Practice reading the time on a clock
questions: What does the clock always say?
What does it do when the hour hand reaches two?
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVIII: The New Scales
steps: New words: orange, scales, beam, groove, gimlet, ribbon
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “First, we must take the peel off.”
Make a simple balance with a hanger, string, and two cups
questions: What did Herbert use for the scale cups?
What did Lucy give him for making them?

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIX: The Bear and the Children
steps: New words: inn, attic, shaggy, eldest, youngest, soldiers
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “See, we are playing soldiers!”
Narrate the story as if you were one of the children
questions: What did the children think the bear was?
What did the bear do when the drum beat?
answers: Rose on his hind legs and danced

lessons.title: Lesson XL: The Little Harebell
steps: New words: harebell, lady, clinging, despair, nodding, blooming
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “God is everywhere.”
Find a picture of a harebell (bluebell)
questions: Where is the harebell growing?
Why isn't the harebell lonely?
answers: On a dreary rock, in the shadow
lessons.notes: Script page: the whole lesson is printed in cursive handwriting (an image in the online text). Read it together, then use a few lines as copywork. It is a short poem.

lessons.title: Lesson XLI: The Fishhawk
steps: New words: osprey, beneath, fiercely, seaside, timidly, robber
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “The eagle is a robber.”
Look up a picture of an osprey
questions: What is another name for the fishhawk?
What does the eagle do to the fishhawk?
answers: Makes him drop his fish and takes it

lessons.title: Lesson XLII: What the Leaf Said
steps: New words: sighing, twig, autumn, October, rustled, trembling
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “Hold on tight.”
Collect fall leaves and sort them by color
questions: What was the leaf afraid of?
Why do the branches keep plain colors?
answers: The wind would pull it off
Their work is not yet done

lessons.title: Lesson XLIII: The Wind and the Leaves
steps: New words: meadows, cricket, farewell, fleecy, whirling, content
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “Come, little leaves.”
Dance like the leaves while you read it
questions: Who called the leaves to come and play?
What covered the leaves at the end?
lessons.notes: Poem by George Cooper. Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIV: Mamma's Present
steps: New words: Christmas, presents, leggings, jolly, expect
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “Just the very thing I wanted most.”
Plan a homemade present for someone
questions: What were the children getting in the woods?
What was mamma's present?
answers: Jessie in a basket of green branches

lessons.title: Lesson XLV: Mary's Story
steps: New words: yesterday, seaweeds, shallow, waded, purple, plumes
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “We went to the beach yesterday.”
Tell a 'yesterday' story of your own, like Mary
questions: What did Mary and Lucy gather?
What funny thing happened to Lucy?
answers: She slipped and fell into the water

lessons.title: Lesson XLVI: Ralph Wick
steps: New words: forget, thorns, snatched, scream, pluck, sore
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “He at last learned to do as he was told.”
Narrate: what did Ralph learn and how?
questions: How old was Ralph?
What happened when he snatched the white rose?

lessons.title: Lesson XLVII: Coasting Down the Hill
steps: New words: coasting, frosty, landscape, laughter, beaming, trudging
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “Coasting down the hill!”
Explain 'coasting' (sledding); talk about sledding or another snow game
questions: What is the weather like?
What do the children do after rushing down the slope?
answers: Frosty, but the sun is bright
Trudge back up through the snow
lessons.notes: Script page: the whole lesson is printed in cursive handwriting (an image in the online text). Read it together, then use a few lines as copywork. It is a poem.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVIII: The Fox and the Ducks
steps: New words: drifting, circling, heed, slyly, cunning, patient
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “The sly old fox”
Narrate the fox's trick step by step
questions: What did the fox send down the river first?
How did the fox catch the ducks?
answers: He hid on a large branch and drifted among them

lessons.title: Lesson XLIX: Pretty Is That Pretty Does
steps: New words: spinner, silken, proverb, poverty, splendor, steady
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “Pretty is which pretty does.”
Talk about what the proverb means
questions: What is the spider planning while she spins?
lessons.notes: Poem by Alice Cary. Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson L: The Story-Teller
steps: New words: civil, appear, travelers, persons, alone
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “Tell us a story we have never heard.”
Predict how the dogs will help someone
questions: What did Ned ask the story to be about?
What are the big dogs taught to do?
answers: Hunt for people lost in the snow
lessons.notes: Part one of a two-part story.

lessons.title: Lesson LI: The Story-Teller (Concluded)
steps: New words: bleak, shrill, lain, stiff, rode
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “He felt something pull him by the coat.”
Narrate the rescue from the boy's point of view
questions: How did the boy get to the men's house?
When did they send him home?
answers: He rode on the dog's back

lessons.title: Lesson LII: The Owl
steps: New words: dusk, squeak, ruffled, awake, creeping
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “Owls can't see very well in the daytime.”
Read it as a conversation in two voices
questions: Where did Harry and Fred find the owl?
How did they catch him?
answers: He was napping in the daytime, and Fred slipped him into a bag
lessons.notes: Part one of a two-part story.

lessons.title: Lesson LIII: The Owl (Concluded)
steps: New words: mouser, ducklings, capture, comical, swallows
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “An owl is a good mouser.”
Tell two facts you learned about owls
questions: What will Harry do with the owl?
Why can the owl surprise its prey?
answers: It flies so softly you can hardly hear it

lessons.title: Lesson LIV: Grandfather's Story
steps: New words: fig, trout, underneath, surprised, fought
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “So much for fighting!”
Compare this story with Lesson XLI, The Fishhawk
questions: What fell from the fig tree?
Why did it fall?
answers: A fishhawk and an eagle fought over it and dropped it

lessons.title: Lesson LV: God Is Great and Good
steps: New words: twinkling, steep, vale, rills, broad
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “For great and good is He.”
List things God made named in the poem
questions: What does the poem say God made to shine at night?
lessons.notes: Poem: read it aloud twice, the second time with expression.

lessons.title: Lesson LVI: A Good Old Man
steps: New words: cottage, hoe, droll, hymn, prayed, grave
Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “Many happy days they spent together.”
Narrate: how did the family take care of one another?
questions: Who lived with the old man?
Who knocked at the door?
answers: His two grandchildren, Mary and Jane

lessons.title: Lesson LVII: The Greedy Girl
steps: New words: greedy, glutton, acorns, doctor, tempers
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “It eats just enough.”
Talk about how the kitten, bee, and squirrel know when to stop
questions: What is a glutton?
What does the bee do with the honey it doesn't eat?
answers: One who eats too much because the food tastes good

lessons.title: Lesson LVIII: A Place for Everything
steps: New words: thimble, borrow, comfort, offended, ashamed
Let your child read the lesson aloud slowly; help only on words they can't sound out
Copywork: “I have a place for everything.”
Read it as a play: one of you is Mary, one is Sarah
questions: What did Mary want to borrow?
What is Sarah's secret?
answers: She has a place for everything and puts everything in its place
lessons.notes: Written as a dialogue.

lessons.title: Lesson LIX: My Mother
steps: New words: constant, lull, rejoice, fretful, meek
Read it once aloud for your child, then have them read it to you (or to a sibling or stuffed animal)
Copywork: “None can love so well as thou.”
Make a card for mother with one line from the poem
questions: What does the child give mother in return?
lessons.notes: Script page: the whole lesson is printed in cursive handwriting (an image in the online text). Read it together, then use a few lines as copywork. It is a poem with old words (thou, thy, didst); explain them as you read.

lessons.title: Lesson LX: The Broken Window

Read the lesson aloud together, pointing to each word; then let your child read it alone
Copywork: “I will go and pay for it.”
Predict: what will happen when George goes back?
questions: What was George's New-year gift?
How did the window break?
answers: His snowball missed James Mason and hit it
lessons.notes: Part one of a two-part story.

lessons.title: Lesson LXI: The Broken Window (Concluded)
steps: New words: merchant, honestly, partner, without
You read a line, then your child reads it back; finish by reading the whole lesson together
Copywork: “He called him an honest boy.”
